name: Sample Guide
source: Synthetic questions written for the app's tests

questions.q: Name the three financial statements and say what each one shows.
questions.a:
The **income statement** shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period.

The **balance sheet** shows assets, liabilities and equity at one point in time.

The **cash flow statement** explains how cash changed over the period.

added.simple: Three statements: profit over a period, what the company owns and owes on one date, and where the cash went.

added.simple: Profit is counted when earned; cash moves when it's collected or paid.
added.example: Revenue 100 on credit, costs 60 paid in cash: net income is 40 before tax, but operating cash is −60 until the 100 is collected.

questions.q: How does a lease show up on the balance sheet?
questions.a: Only long leases that work like a purchase go on the balance sheet. Other leases are just rent: an operating expense, with nothing recorded as an asset or a liability.

added.simple: Today almost every lease longer than a year is on the balance sheet.

update.why: A newer standard put nearly all leases on the balance sheet.
update.text: Leases longer than 12 months now show a right-of-use asset and a lease liability, whether they are finance or operating leases.

questions.q: What do these discount periods look like with a half-year stub?
questions.a:
Here is the pattern:

```table
 | Stub | Year 1 | Year 2
Normal: | 0.5 | 1.5 | 2.5
Mid-year: | 0.25 | 1 | 2
Note: | Same | < | <
```

The stub is halved; later years drop by 0.5.

questions.q: What is 3 \* 4 written with an escaped asterisk?
questions.a: It is 3 \* 4 = 12, and this stays as text.

questions.q: What's the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
questions.a: Equity value belongs to shareholders. Enterprise value is the value of the operations to every capital provider.

added.simple: Equity value is for shareholders; enterprise value is for everyone who funds the business.

questions.q: Should you subtract all of a company's cash when you calculate enterprise value?
questions.a: Usually yes, but cash the business needs to operate is arguably part of its operations.

questions.q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 together and the bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball?
questions.a: 5 cents. If the ball is x, the bat is x + 1.00, so 2x + 1.00 = 1.10 and x = 0.05.

added.simple: Set the ball to x and solve; the instinctive 10 cents is wrong.
